config.title: Build optimistic UI for add and delete actions

intro.title: Build optimistic UI for add and delete actions
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple task list application that instantly updates the user interface when adding or deleting items, before the server confirms the action. You will learn the core concept of optimistic UI, which improves perceived performance by assuming operations will succeed. The main technologies involved are JavaScript for state management and DOM manipulation to reflect changes immediately. This approach provides a smoother, more responsive experience for users interacting with dynamic content.
intro.usecase: Optimistic UI is essential for creating responsive interfaces in modern web applications. You'll see this pattern in social media platforms where posts appear instantly when you click 'Post' while the server processes in the background, or in e-commerce carts where items disappear immediately when you click 'Remove' before the backend update completes. This approach is crucial for dashboards, task management tools, and collaborative apps where users expect immediate visual feedback for their actions, reducing perceived latency and improving the overall user experience.

objectives: Construct a function to simulate server requests for add and delete operations
Initialize state variables to track pending UI updates and server synchronization status
Implement optimistic UI updates by immediately modifying the local state before server confirmation
Configure error handling to revert optimistic updates when server requests fail
Integrate loading indicators to reflect the pending state of optimistic operations
Manipulate the DOM to reflect both optimistic updates and final server-confirmed states
Apply conditional rendering to differentiate between optimistic and confirmed data states

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.

import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have access to React and the useState hook for managing state in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main App component

steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function called App that returns an empty fragment: <> </> or <React.Fragment> </React.Fragment>.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty fragment.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is created and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't quite right. Create a functional component named App that returns an empty fragment.

steps.title: Initialize state for the todo list
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'todos' initialized with an empty array.
steps.hint: Call useState with [] as the initial value and destructure the returned array into 'todos' and 'setTodos'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state with an array
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a todos state variable ready to store todo items.
successCriteria: The App component contains a useState call that initializes 'todos' with an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState and initializing the todos variable with an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the App component, use useState to create a state variable named 'todos' initialized with an empty array.

steps.title: Initialize state for the new todo input
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable called 'newTodo' initialized with an empty string.
steps.hint: Add another useState call after your existing todos state. The pattern is: const [newTodo, setNewTodo] = useState('');
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a state variable for input
const [inputValue, setInputValue] = useState('');
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: 'todos' for the list and 'newTodo' for the current input value.
successCriteria: The 'newTodo' state variable is declared with useState and initialized with an empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState to create a variable called 'newTodo' with an initial value of empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a second useState call to create the 'newTodo' state variable.

steps.title: Create the handleAddTodo function
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, create a function named handleAddTodo that will handle adding new todos. For now, just define the function with an empty body.
steps.hint: You can write either a function declaration or an arrow function. Place it after the state declarations but before the return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now contains a handleAddTodo function definition, ready to be filled with optimistic update logic in later steps.
successCriteria: A function named handleAddTodo is defined inside the App component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a function named handleAddTodo inside the App component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleAddTodo function is not defined correctly. Please create a function named handleAddTodo inside the App component.

steps.title: Create the handleDeleteTodo function
steps.instruction: Create a function named handleDeleteTodo that takes a todo id parameter. Inside the function, immediately remove that todo from the todos state using setTodos, store the removed todo in a variable, and simulate an API call with setTimeout that logs 'Delete successful' after 1 second.
steps.hint: You can use setTodos with the previous state to filter out the todo with the matching id. Store the removed todo before filtering so you have it for potential rollback.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleDeleteTodo function is defined with optimistic removal and simulated API call.
successCriteria: handleDeleteTodo function exists, takes an id parameter, immediately updates todos state, stores the removed todo, and has setTimeout that logs after 1 second.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes an id parameter, removes the todo from state immediately, and includes the setTimeout simulation.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the function name and structure. You need to create handleDeleteTodo with id parameter, update state optimistically, and simulate API call.

steps.title: Add the main container and input field
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, replace the current 'return null' with a main container div that contains an input field for adding new todos.
steps.hint: Start by returning a div element. Inside that div, add an input element with type='text' and placeholder='Add a new todo'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a basic structure with a container div and an input field, ready to be connected to state and handlers in later steps.
successCriteria: The component returns a div containing an input element with type='text' and a placeholder attribute.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a div that contains an input element with type='text' and a placeholder.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've replaced 'return null' with a div containing an input element. The input should have type='text' and a placeholder attribute.

steps.title: Add the Add Todo button and wire it
steps.instruction: Add a button element next to the input field with the text 'Add Todo' and wire its onClick handler to call the handleAddTodo function.
steps.hint: Place the button after the input element inside the same container. Use the onClick attribute to call your handler function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with click handler
<button onClick={handleSubmit}>Submit</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Add Todo' appears next to the input field, and clicking it will trigger the handleAddTodo function (which will be implemented in later steps).
successCriteria: Button element is present with text 'Add Todo'
Button has onClick handler calling handleAddTodo
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it has the correct text 'Add Todo' and the onClick handler calls handleAddTodo.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured. Check that you've added a button element with the correct text and onClick handler.

steps.title: Display the list of todos
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement, add a <ul> element after the button. Inside the <ul>, map over the 'todos' state array to render each todo's text in an <li> element.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the todos array. For each todo object, return an <li> element containing the todo's text property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The todos array will be displayed as a bulleted list below the input and button.
successCriteria: A <ul> element is added after the button, containing <li> elements for each todo in the state array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the map method on the todos array and returning <li> elements with the todo text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The todo list isn't displaying correctly. Check that you've added the <ul> element and used the map method properly.

steps.title: Add Delete buttons to each todo
steps.instruction: Inside the map function that renders each todo item, add a Delete button element with an onClick handler that calls handleDeleteTodo with that todo's id.
steps.hint: You'll need to add a <button> element inside the existing JSX for each todo. Use onClick={() => handleDeleteTodo(todo.id)} to wire the click event.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each todo item in the list will now have a Delete button next to it that, when clicked, will trigger the delete functionality.
successCriteria: Each todo list item contains a Delete button with an onClick handler that calls handleDeleteTodo with the todo's id.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a Delete button, but check that it's inside the map function for each todo and that the onClick handler correctly passes todo.id to handleDeleteTodo.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Delete buttons aren't properly added. Make sure you add a <button> element inside the todo.map() JSX with onClick={() => handleDeleteTodo(todo.id)}.

steps.title: Add visual feedback during optimistic updates
steps.instruction: Add a loading state variable and disable the Add Todo button when a todo is being added.
steps.hint: Create a new state variable to track when an add operation is in progress, then add the disabled attribute to the button.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Add Todo button should be disabled and show 'Adding...' text while a todo is being added.
successCriteria: Add Todo button has disabled attribute set to isAdding
Button text changes to 'Adding...' when disabled
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've added both the disabled attribute and updated the button text to show 'Adding...' when isAdding is true.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding a state variable to track when adding is in progress, then use it to disable the Add Todo button and change its text.

steps.title: Add error handling for failed deletes
steps.instruction: In the handleDeleteTodo function, store the todo being deleted in a variable before removing it,
steps.hint: Before calling setTodos to filter out the todo, save it in a variable like 'deletedTodo'. Inside setTimeout, use Math.random() to simulate failure and call setTodos to add the todo back if random < 0.3.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleDeleteTodo function now stores the todo before deletion and has a setTimeout that simulates occasional failure (30% chance) and reverts the state by adding the todo back if the delete fails.
successCriteria: The handleDeleteTodo function stores the todo being deleted in a variable before filtering
A setTimeout is added after the optimistic update
Inside setTimeout, Math.random() is used to simulate failure
If random < 0.3, setTodos is called to add the stored todo back
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're storing the todo before deleting it and using setTimeout with Math.random() to simulate failure and revert if needed.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleDeleteTodo function needs to store the todo before deletion and include a setTimeout that simulates occasional failure with rollback. Check the analogous example for guidance.
